subject: math

unit.title: Statistics, shape and symmetry
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we record data, and how do we describe shapes by their parts and their symmetry?

title: Block diagrams: most, least, how many more
objectives: By the end, I can read a block diagram to answer 'most', 'least' and 'how many more'.

vocabulary.definition: a chart where every count is one block, stacked into bars
the biggest amount — the tallest bar
the smallest amount — the shortest bar
the gap between two bars — find it by subtracting
two or more bars added together

emphasize: The TALLEST bar is the most; the shortest is the least.
'How many more' means find the DIFFERENCE — subtract the two bars, never add them.
Read a bar by its TOP: finger on the top block, read across to the number.

misconceptions: reading 'how many more' as 'how many altogether' and adding (6 and 4 → 10 instead of 2)
misreading a bar's height by not tracking from its top across to the scale
answering 'most' with the category they like best instead of the tallest bar
hooks: Which colour car passes the window the most? We could argue — or we could chart it and KNOW.

digital: animated block diagram on the whiteboard (one rect per block)

plan.goal: Frame the chart as the argument-settler; retrieve difference by subtraction.
plan.note: The retrieval question (6 and 4 → 2 more) is the exact calculation the whole lesson runs on.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers '2' for 'I have 6, you have 4 — how many more do I have?'

script.say: Here's an argument: which colour car passes the window the most? We could shout about it… or we could chart it and KNOW. I watched the street and counted every car — the chart's coming up. But first, quick memory check: if I have 6 stickers and you have 4, how many MORE do I have?
script.adaptHints: Swap cars for whatever passes the child's window (buses, dogs, bikes) and stickers for their favourite collectable. Listen for '2' — and for HOW they got it.

blocks.caption: Which colour passes most? Chart it and KNOW.

stuckProtocol: If 'how many more' stalls: line up 6 fingers against 4 fingers and count the ones sticking out — the gap is the answer.

plan.goal: Model reading the car chart: one block = one car, tallest bar = most, and 'how many more' = subtract two bars.
plan.note: Build the chart block by block so 'one block = one count' lands. Then do one full 'how many more' with the subtraction written out, and one total.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees red (6) named as most because it's tallest, and hears 6 − 4 = 2 for 'how many more red than blue'.

script.say: Here's my car chart. Every block is ONE car — watch them stack. Red: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Blue: 4. Green: 5. White: 2. Now the chart does the talking! The TALLEST bar is the most — red wins with 6. The shortest is the least — poor white, only 2. And here's the power move: how many MORE red than blue? I compare the two bars and SUBTRACT: 6 take away 4 is 2. Two more red cars. And if I want red and white TOGETHER, I add: 6 plus 2 is 8.
script.adaptHints: Count each block aloud as it appears. Point at the bar TOPS when comparing — model the finger-on-top habit.

plan.goal: Shared read of the same chart: child names most and least, then computes 'how many more green than white' with scribed subtraction.
plan.note: The character scribes the calculation the child dictates: 5 − 2 = 3. Keep fingers on the bar tops.
plan.successCriteria: Child names red as most, white as least, and says 5 − 2 = 3 for green vs white.

script.say: Your turn on the same chart. Put your finger on the tallest bar… which colour is the MOST? … And the shortest — the least? … Now the power move: how many more GREEN than WHITE? Read the tops: green is 5, white is 2. Tell me the subtraction and I'll write it down.
script.adaptHints: If the child says '7' (adding), don't correct — ask 'is the gap between the bars really bigger than the green bar itself?'

check.question: Green = 5, white = 2 — how many more green cars than white?

wrongAnswers.why: read 'how many more' as 'how many altogether' and added
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'More' asks about the GAP between the bars. Look at the blocks green has that white doesn't — count just those.

wrongAnswers.why: read the taller bar's height as the answer
wrongAnswers.remedy: 5 is how many green cars there are. But the question wants how many EXTRA green has compared to white — compare the two bars.

plan.goal: Diagnose 'how many more' on a fresh chart: dogs 6, cats 4 → 2 more dogs.
plan.note: The lesson's key diagnostic. '10' = added instead of subtracted; re-run the line-them-up-count-the-gap move.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 2 and can name which two bars they compared.

script.say: New chart — pets this time! Dogs have 6 blocks, cats have 4. Question: how many MORE dogs than cats? Think about what 'more' asks you to do…
script.adaptHints: After a correct answer, probe: 'Which two bars did you compare? How did you find the gap?'

blocks.caption: Pets in our street — every block is 1 pet

blocks.prompt: Dogs = 6, cats = 4. How many MORE dogs than cats?
blocks.explain: 'How many more' is the gap: 6 − 4 = 2. Two more dogs.

check.question: Dogs = 6, cats = 4 — how many more dogs than cats?

wrongAnswers.why: added the bars — read 'more' as 'altogether'
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Altogether' would be adding. 'How many MORE' wants the gap. Line the bars up — how many blocks stick out past the cats?

wrongAnswers.why: gave the taller bar's height instead of the difference
wrongAnswers.remedy: 6 is the dogs' whole bar. The question asks how many EXTRA blocks the dogs have — compare the two tops.

plan.goal: Independent most/least/how-many-more reads across fresh charts; once secure, interleave totals and a build-from-tally item.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. Watch for adding on 'more' questions and misread bar heights. Two-step items are the level-3 goal.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 3+ items correctly including one 'how many more' by subtraction and one total by addition.

script.say: Practice time, chart champion! Fresh charts, tricky questions — most, least, how many more, and the odd 'altogether' hiding in there to keep you sharp. Read the tops, choose your sum!
script.adaptHints: Re-theme the charts to the child's interests (dinosaur species spotted, goals per team, minibeasts found). Keep every number identical.

stuckProtocol: Name why: ''more' got read as 'altogether'' or 'a bar top got misread.'
Redraw the two bars side by side and count ONLY the blocks that stick out past the shorter bar.
One hint: ''How many more' means the difference — the gap.'
Re-ask with tiny bars (5 and 3), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states the two rules — tallest = most, 'how many more' = subtract; end on a win.
plan.successCriteria: Child says ''how many more' means subtract / find the difference' in their own words.

script.say: Chart wisdom time! How do you spot the MOST on a block diagram? … And what does 'how many more' tell you to do? … Exactly — compare the bars and subtract. You read the tops of the bars carefully and picked the right sum every time — that's clear data thinking, the same thinking scientists use.
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: finger on the bar tops, choosing subtract vs add, self-correcting an 'altogether' slip.

block.prompt: Pets chart: dogs 6 blocks, cats 4 blocks, fish 2 blocks. Which pet is the MOST?
block.explain: Dogs have the tallest bar — 6 blocks. Tallest bar = most.

wrongAnswers.why: picked a middle bar — didn't compare all the tops
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at all three bar tops. Which one reaches highest?

wrongAnswers.why: possibly picked their favourite instead of reading the chart
wrongAnswers.remedy: The chart doesn't care what we like best! Which bar has the most blocks stacked up?

hints: Count the blocks in each bar if you're not sure.

reteach.say: 'Most' is a height contest between the bars. Stand them side by side: dogs 6, cats 4, fish 2. The dogs' tower reaches highest — dogs are the most. Shortest tower — fish — is the least.

block.prompt: Fruit chart: the bananas bar has blocks stacked to the 5. How many bananas were counted?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the gaps or stopped one block short
wrongAnswers.remedy: Touch every block from the bottom to the top: 1, 2, 3… don't stop until your finger is on the very top block.

wrongAnswers.why: counted past the top or included the label
wrongAnswers.remedy: Finger on the TOP block, then read straight across to the number line. Where does it point?

hints: Finger on the top block, read across to the number.

reteach.say: Reading a bar is a lift ride: start at the bottom, count each block as you rise — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — and STOP at the top. The top block tells the truth: 5 bananas.

block.caption: Count blocks bottom to top, stop at the top

block.prompt: Dogs = 6, cats = 4. How many MORE dogs than cats?

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of finding the difference
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'More' asks for the gap, not the pile. Line the bars up — how many dog blocks stick out past the cats?

wrongAnswers.why: gave the bigger bar's height
wrongAnswers.remedy: That's ALL the dogs. We want just the extra ones — the blocks above the cats' line.

reteach.say: Stand the bars next to each other. Cats reach 4, dogs reach 6 — the two dog blocks poking out above the cats' line ARE the answer. That poking-out bit is the difference: 6 − 4 = 2.

block.caption: The blocks that stick out = how many more (2)

block.prompt: Dogs = 6, fish = 2. How many dogs and fish ALTOGETHER?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted — mixed up 'altogether' with 'how many more'
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Altogether' means join both bars into one big pile. 6 and 2 joined make…?

wrongAnswers.why: gave one bar and forgot to add the other
wrongAnswers.remedy: Both pets count! Start at 6 dogs and count on the 2 fish: 7, 8.

reteach.say: Two magic words, two different sums: 'how many MORE' means subtract the bars; 'ALTOGETHER' means add them. This one says altogether — stack both bars into one mega-bar: 6 + 2 = 8.

block.caption: Let the question word pick the sum

block.prompt: Car chart: red = 7, blue = 4. How many more red cars than blue?

wrongAnswers.why: added the two bars
wrongAnswers.remedy: 11 would answer 'how many altogether'. 'How many more' wants the gap — take the blue bar away from the red bar.

wrongAnswers.why: read the taller bar as the answer
wrongAnswers.remedy: 7 is the whole red bar. How many of those red blocks are ABOVE where the blue bar stops?

reteach.say: Picture red and blue racing up the chart. Blue stops at 4; red keeps climbing — 5, 6, 7. Count the climbs red made after blue stopped: three. That's 7 − 4 = 3 more red cars.

practiceBank.skill: read a chart from emoji bars

block.prompt: Minibeast hunt! Ants ⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛, spiders ⬛⬛⬛, worms ⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛. Which is the LEAST?
block.explain: Spiders have the shortest bar — only 3 blocks. Shortest = least.

wrongAnswers.why: muddled most and least
wrongAnswers.remedy: Least means the SMALLEST amount. Which bar is shortest?

wrongAnswers.why: compared only two of the bars
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check all three: ants 7, worms 5, spiders 3. Which number is smallest?

reteach.say: Line the bars up like towers: ants built 7, worms built 5, spiders only managed 3. The shortest tower is the least — spiders. Most and least are just tallest and shortest in disguise.

block.prompt: Match each chart question to what you do.

pairs.left: How many more dogs than cats?

wrongAnswers.answer: How many more dogs than cats? → add the bars
wrongAnswers.why: the add-on-'more' trap
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'More' compares — it wants the gap between the bars, and gaps come from subtracting.

hints: 'More' compares two bars — that's a difference.

reteach.say: Chart questions are a code: MOST — scan for the tallest. LEAST — the shortest. ALTOGETHER — add bars into one pile. HOW MANY MORE — subtract to find the gap. Crack the word, and the chart does the rest.

steps: Read the question word: most / least / altogether / how many more.
Most or least → compare bar heights.
How many more → subtract the bars.

block.prompt: Chart: red cars = 7, white cars = 2. Answer BOTH: how many more red than white, AND how many red and white altogether?

wrongAnswers.why: swapped the operations — added for 'more' and subtracted for 'altogether'
wrongAnswers.remedy: Match the words to the sums: 'more' is the gap (subtract), 'altogether' is the pile (add). Try each again.

wrongAnswers.why: answered the first part and reused it
wrongAnswers.remedy: Two different questions need two different sums. 'Altogether' joins BOTH bars — 7 and 2 make…?

hints: Do them one at a time: gap first, then pile.

reteach.say: Same two bars, two different questions! The gap: red reaches 5 blocks past white — 7 − 2 = 5 more. The pile: push both bars together — 7 + 2 = 9 altogether. One chart can answer lots of questions if you pick the right sum each time.

practiceBank.skill: build a block diagram from a tally

block.prompt: You tallied bikes: one gate of 5 and 1 more. How tall should the bikes bar be on your block diagram?
block.explain: The tally says 6 (gate of 5 + 1), so the bar gets 6 blocks — one block per bike.

wrongAnswers.why: counted the gate but dropped the extra stroke
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count the tally again: the gate is 5, then count on the loose strokes. Every bike gets a block.

wrongAnswers.why: drew one block per tally GROUP instead of per count
wrongAnswers.remedy: Blocks aren't for groups — one block = one bike. How many bikes did the tally count in total?

hints: First read the tally: gate + strokes = ?
One block for every single bike.

reteach.say: Tally to chart is a relay race: first the tally hands over its total — gate of 5 plus 1 is 6. Then the chart stacks exactly that many blocks — 6 blocks, one per bike. The total travels; nothing gets lost on the way.

steps: Read the tally total (gates in 5s, then strokes).
Stack exactly that many blocks — one block per count.

block.statement: To answer 'how many more dogs than cats?', you ADD the dogs bar and the cats bar.
block.explain: 'How many more' is the gap between the bars — subtract: dogs − cats.

wrongAnswers.why: the lesson's core misconception — 'more' read as 'altogether'
wrongAnswers.remedy: Adding answers a different question ('altogether'). Line the bars up — is the gap between them found by piling them together, or by taking one from the other?

hints: Does 'more' ask about the pile, or the gap?

reteach.say: Watch the trap word: MORE. If dogs have 6 and cats have 4, piling them up gives 10 — but that answers 'altogether'. The gap between the bars is 6 − 4 = 2. 'How many more' always wants the gap.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave 'how many more', totals and build-from-tally items so the child picks the operation each time.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the two bars redrawn side by side and the sticking-out blocks counted together, then serve a level-1 item.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one 'how many more' answered by subtraction and one 'altogether' answered by addition → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'reading block diagrams'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'more' read as 'altogether', or a bar top misread.
Redraw the two bars side by side; count only the blocks that stick out.
One hint: ''more' means the difference — the gap.'
Re-ask with bars of 5 and 3, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Re-theme every chart to the learner's world (LearnerModel.interests): goals per team, dinosaurs spotted, cars past THEIR window. Numbers and questions stay identical.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable most/least read, then specific process praise: 'you read the bar tops and chose subtract for the gap — that's proper data thinking.'

differentiation.support: Finger on each bar's top and read across; bars capped at 6; the question word (more/altogether) highlighted before answering.
differentiation.stretch: Build a block diagram from a tally chart; two-step questions ('how many more, AND the total'); ask the child to write their own chart question.

extension: Real-data chart — tally cars (or birds, or passers-by) out the window for two minutes, then build the block diagram and ask a 'how many more' question about it.
assessmentEvidence: Child reads most/least from bar heights and finds 'how many more' by subtracting two bars (not adding), plus one total by addition.
revisitLater: Chart reading returns in the Lesson 25 quiz and in Unit 8 mixed problems; keep one 'more vs altogether' contrast item in the next two starters.
